warmup.q: A fee endpoint's average latency is 0.6 µs and its p99 is 3.9 µs, but its p99.99 is 13.6 ms. The service runs 130 garbage collections in 15 seconds. Where do you look first?
options: The database, since slow requests are usually I/O
Allocation: the rare slow calls are most likely waiting for GC pauses, and the GC runs because the code allocates a lot
The JIT: 13.6 ms is a compilation
warmup.why: Most calls are fast, and a few are three or four orders of magnitude slower. With 130 GCs in 15 seconds, the obvious suspect is a call that happens to wait for a stop-the-world pause. Fewer allocations mean fewer collections. There's no database in a fee calculation, and while compilation can slow early calls, it doesn't happen 130 times.

sections.h: Start from the symptom: the tail and the GC, not the average
sections.html:
Here is the complaint, measured. Four threads call a card-fee calculation as fast as they can for 15 seconds, with a 256 MB heap, and every call is timed into a histogram. These are the research run's numbers on JDK 21:

604,529 calls/s   p50 < 0.7 us   p99 < 3.9 us   p99.9 < 35.3 us   p99.99 < 13.6 ms
130 GCs, 996 ms of GC time

The average is excellent. One call in ten thousand takes over 13 ms, which in a payment API is the difference between a smooth checkout and a timeout somewhere upstream. jfr view gc-pauses on the same run said 129 pauses, 984 ms in total, median 2.98 ms. That's the first hypothesis: the slow calls are the ones that hit a pause, and the pauses happen because the code allocates.

The code looks harmless:

Java
static long feeSlow(Payment p) {
    if (!Pattern.compile("^[A-Z]{3}$").matcher(p.currency()).matches())   // line 19
        throw new IllegalArgumentException("bad currency");
    BigDecimal amount = new BigDecimal(p.amount());
    BigDecimal fee = amount.multiply(new BigDecimal("0.029")).add(new BigDecimal("0.30"))  // line 22
            .setScale(2, RoundingMode.HALF_EVEN);
    debug(String.format("payment %s merchant=%s amount=%s fee=%s",        // line 24
            p.id(), p.merchant(), amount.toPlainString(), fee.toPlainString()));
    return fee.unscaledValue().longValue();
}
Kotlin
fun ktFeeSlow(p: KtPayment): Long {
    require(Regex("^[A-Z]{3}$").matches(p.currency)) { "bad currency" }   // a regex per call
    val amount = BigDecimal(p.amount)
    val fee = (amount * BigDecimal("0.029") + BigDecimal("0.30"))         // constants per call
        .setScale(2, RoundingMode.HALF_EVEN)
    ktDebug("payment %s merchant=%s amount=%s fee=%s"                      // formatted, then dropped
        .format(p.id, p.merchant, amount.toPlainString(), fee.toPlainString()))
    return fee.unscaledValue().toLong()
}

It returns the right fee. Three costs hide in it: a regex compiled on every call, two BigDecimal constants built on every call, and a DEBUG log line formatted on every call and then dropped because DEBUG is off.

One caution before you change anything. The maximum latency stayed between 0.37 and 0.53 seconds in every version of this code, before and after the fixes. On a shared machine with four busy threads on four vCPUs, plus GC and JIT threads, the operating system sometimes doesn't schedule a thread for a while. Don't present the max as an effect of your fix. The percentiles are the evidence.

code.title: FeeInvestigation.java
code.html: package workbench.performance.l07; import jdk.jfr.consumer.RecordedEvent; import jdk.jfr.consumer.RecordedFrame; import jdk.jfr.consumer.RecordingFile; import java.lang.management.GarbageCollectorMXBean; import java.lang.management.ManagementFactory; import java.nio.file.Path; import java.util.ArrayList; import java.util.HashMap; import java.util.List; import java.util.Map; import java.util.function.ToLongFunction; /** * Runs one fee variant (slow, hoisted or noregex) on 4 threads for 3 seconds in a second JVM with * -Xmx256m and a JFR recording, prints latency percentiles and GC counts, then reads the recording * and prints allocation by source line in this package. Usage: -Pargs=slow (or hoisted, noregex). */ public class FeeInvestigation { public static void main(String[] args) throws Exception { String mode = args.length > 0 ? args[0] : "slow"; if (args.length > 1 && args[1].equals("child")) { load(mode); return; } Path file = Path.of("build", "fees-" + mode + ".jfr").toAbsolutePath(); String java = ProcessHandle.current().info().command().orElse("java"); Process p = new ProcessBuilder(java, "-Xmx256m", "-Xlog:jfr+startup=warning", "-XX:StartFlightRecording:filename=" + file + ",settings=profile", "-cp", System.getProperty("java.class.path"), FeeInvestigation.class.getName(), mode, "child") .inheritIO().start(); p.waitFor(); allocationByLine(file); } // the load: 4 threads, each timing every call into a fixed histogram (no allocation of its own) static void load(String mode) throws Exception { ToLongFunction<FeeVariants.Payment> fee = switch (mode) { case "slow" -> FeeVariants::feeSlow; case "hoisted" -> FeeVariants::feeHoisted; default -> FeeVariants::feeNoRegex; }; FeeVariants.Payment[] ps = FeeVariants.payments(4_096); long end = System.nanoTime() + 3_000_000_000L; long[][] hist = new long[4][]; List<Thread> threads = new ArrayList<>(); for (int t = 0; t < 4; t++) { int id = t; Thread th = new Thread(() -> { long[] h = new long[20_001]; // 100 ns buckets up to 1 ms, then 100 us buckets up to 1 s long sink = 0; for (int i = id; System.nanoTime() < end; i++) { long t0 = System.nanoTime(); sink += fee.applyAsLong(ps[i & 4095]); long d = System.nanoTime() - t0; h[d < 1_000_000 ? (int) (d / 100) : (int) Math.min(20_000, 10_000 + (d - 1_000_000) / 100_000)]++; } hist[id] = h; if (sink == 42) System.out.println(); }); th.start(); threads.add(th); } for (Thread th : threads) th.join(); long[] h = new long[20_001]; for (long[] x : hist) for (int k = 0; k < h.length; k++) h[k] += x[k]; long total = 0; for (long n : h) total += n; long gcs = 0, gcMs = 0; for (GarbageCollectorMXBean gc : ManagementFactory.getGarbageCollectorMXBeans()) { gcs += gc.getCollectionCount(); gcMs += gc.getCollectionTime(); } System.out.printf("%s: %,d calls/s p50 %s p99 %s p99.9 %s p99.99 %s GCs %d (%d ms)%n", mode, total / 3, pct(h, total, 0.5), pct(h, total, 0.99), pct(h, total, 0.999), pct(h, total, 0.9999), gcs, gcMs); } static String pct(long[] h, long total, double q) { long target = (long) Math.ceil(total * q), acc = 0; for (int k = 0; k < h.length; k++) { acc += h[k]; if (acc >= target) return k < 10_000 ? "<" + (k + 1) * 100 + "ns" : "<" + ((k - 10_000 + 1) * 100 + 1_000) + "us"; } return "?"; } // what `jfr view allocation-by-site` can't tell you: the line in YOUR code each sample came from static void allocationByLine(Path file) throws Exception { Map<String, Long> weight = new HashMap<>(); long total = 0; for (RecordedEvent e : RecordingFile.readAllEvents(file)) { if (!e.getEventType().getName().equals("jdk.ObjectAllocationSample") || e.getStackTrace() == null) continue; for (RecordedFrame f : e.getStackTrace().getFrames()) { if (f.getMethod().getType().getName().startsWith("workbench.performance.l07.FeeVariants")) { weight.merge(f.getMethod().getName() + " line " + f.getLineNumber(), e.getLong("weight"), Long::sum); total += e.getLong("weight"); break; // the first frame in our code is the one to change } } } long sum = total; System.out.println("allocation by line in FeeVariants.java (from " + file.getFileName() + "):"); weight.entrySet().stream().sorted(Map.Entry.<String, Long>comparingByValue().reversed()).limit(5) .forEach(en -> System.out.printf(" %5.1f%% %s%n", 100.0 * en.getValue() / sum, en.getKey())); } }

try.expect: Around a million to four million calls per second on a laptop-class machine, p50 well under a microsecond, and a p99.99 hundreds or thousands of times the p50. Dozens of GCs or more in 3 seconds. The allocation by line puts lines 24 and 19 (String.format and Pattern.compile) at the top with about a third each, then line 25 (the toPlainString arguments) and line 22 (the constants). The latency numbers move a lot from run to run on a busy machine; the allocation shares hardly move.

sections.h: JFR names the allocation, and the first line in your code names the fix
sections.html:
jfr view allocation-by-site on the slow run answers "what allocates" in JDK terms:

Formatter.parse              12.48%
Pattern.compile()            10.34%
PaymentSim.feeSlow           10.12%
Arrays.copyOf                 7.92%
Pattern$BitClass.<init>       7.80%
Matcher.<init>                7.44%

That's real, and not yet useful: you can't change Formatter.parse. The view groups by the top frame, the method that did the allocating. What you want is the first frame in your own code under it. Each jdk.ObjectAllocationSample event carries a stack trace and a weight (how many bytes the sample stands for), so a few lines of RecordingFile, as in lesson 5's lab, can group by your file and line instead. FeeInvestigation does that. One run:

allocation by line in FeeVariants.java (from fees-slow.jfr):
   36.0%  feeSlow line 24      String.format(...) for the dropped log line
   32.6%  feeSlow line 19      Pattern.compile(...)
   19.1%  feeSlow line 25      toPlainString() arguments for the log line
    9.2%  feeSlow line 22      new BigDecimal("0.029"), new BigDecimal("0.30")

The research run's own parser got the same order: 34.7% on the regex line, 31.9% on String.format, 15.9% on the toPlainString arguments, 8.9% on the constants. More than half of all allocation is a log line nobody reads.

A flame graph answers the next question: who calls the allocating code, and through which path. In lesson 6's allocation profile of the same code, Pattern.compile held 37.4% of the allocated bytes and String.format 27.9%. Two independent tools agree, which is the point of using both. JFR is built in and cheap enough to leave running. async-profiler gives you the full picture, native and JVM frames included, when you can attach it.

The figure shows the loop this lesson follows. The step people skip is the dashed one.

sections.h: Fix one thing, then profile again
sections.html:
Round 1 fixes the three obvious costs: the pattern and the two constants become static final fields, and the log line is formatted only when DEBUG is on. The research run went from 604,529 to 3,355,692 calls per second, p99.99 fell from under 13.6 ms to under 35.6 µs, and the GC count from 130 to 79.

Then profile again, because the picture has changed. FeeInvestigation -Pargs=hoisted here:

allocation by line in FeeVariants.java (from fees-hoisted.jfr):
   75.4%  feeHoisted line 35      CCY.matcher(p.currency()).matches()
   24.0%  feeHoisted line 36      new BigDecimal(p.amount())

The research run put 94.8% on the same line. A precompiled Pattern still creates a new Matcher object on every call. That cost was there from the start, hidden under bigger ones. It only became the top line after round 1. Checking three letters doesn't need a regex at all, so round 2 replaces it with a plain loop:

Java
static final BigDecimal RATE = new BigDecimal("0.029");      // round 1: built once
static final BigDecimal FIXED = new BigDecimal("0.30");

static boolean isCurrencyCode(String s) {                     // round 2: no regex for 3 letters
    if (s.length() != 3) return false;
    for (int i = 0; i < 3; i++) {
        char c = s.charAt(i);
        if (c < 'A' || c > 'Z') return false;
    }
    return true;
}

static long feeNoRegex(Payment p) {
    if (!isCurrencyCode(p.currency())) throw new IllegalArgumentException("bad currency");
    BigDecimal amount = new BigDecimal(p.amount());           // the work that's left
    BigDecimal fee = amount.multiply(RATE).add(FIXED).setScale(2, RoundingMode.HALF_EVEN);
    if (debugEnabled) debug(String.format("payment %s merchant=%s amount=%s fee=%s",   // round 1: guarded
            p.id(), p.merchant(), amount.toPlainString(), fee.toPlainString()));
    return fee.unscaledValue().longValue();
}
Kotlin
val KT_RATE = BigDecimal("0.029")                            // round 1: built once
val KT_FIXED = BigDecimal("0.30")

fun isCurrencyCodeKt(s: String) = s.length == 3 && s.all { it in 'A'..'Z' }   // round 2: no regex

fun ktFeeNoRegex(p: KtPayment): Long {
    require(isCurrencyCodeKt(p.currency)) { "bad currency" }
    val amount = BigDecimal(p.amount)                         // the work that's left
    val fee = (amount * KT_RATE + KT_FIXED).setScale(2, RoundingMode.HALF_EVEN)
    if (ktDebugEnabled) ktDebug("payment %s merchant=%s amount=%s fee=%s"   // round 1: guarded
        .format(p.id, p.merchant, amount.toPlainString(), fee.toPlainString()))
    return fee.unscaledValue().toLong()
}

After round 2 the research run did 4,292,668 calls per second, p99.99 under 28.4 µs, and 37 GCs. The re-profile here shows 99.9% of what's left on one line, new BigDecimal(p.amount()), parsing the amount string. That's the actual job, so this is where to stop, unless a budget says otherwise. Parsing cents by hand would remove it, and would also add rounding and validation code that someone has to get right.

Three habits come out of this. Fix one thing at a time, so you know what each change did. Profile after every fix, because the order of costs changes. And stop when the top of the profile is the work the code exists to do.

Check yourself: in round 1 you hoist the Pattern but forget the log guard. Which line will lead the next profile? (The String.format line: about a third of the original allocation, and now the biggest share.)

"<" + (k + 1) * 100 + "ns" : "<" + ((k - 10_000 + 1) * 100 + 1_000) + "us"; } return "?"; } // what `jfr view allocation-by-site` can't tell you: the line in YOUR code each sample came from static void allocationByLine(Path file) throws Exception { Map<String, Long> weight = new HashMap<>(); long total = 0; for (RecordedEvent e : RecordingFile.readAllEvents(file)) { if (!e.getEventType().getName().equals("jdk.ObjectAllocationSample") || e.getStackTrace() == null) continue; for (RecordedFrame f : e.getStackTrace().getFrames()) { if (f.getMethod().getType().getName().startsWith("workbench.performance.l07.FeeVariants")) { weight.merge(f.getMethod().getName() + " line " + f.getLineNumber(), e.getLong("weight"), Long::sum); total += e.getLong("weight"); break; // the first frame in our code is the one to change } } } long sum = total; System.out.println("allocation by line in FeeVariants.java (from " + file.getFileName() + "):"); weight.entrySet().stream().sorted(Map.Entry.<String, Long>comparingByValue().reversed()).limit(5) .forEach(en -> System.out.printf(" %5.1f%% %s%n", 100.0 * en.getValue() / sum, en.getKey())); } }

try.expect: hoisted puts most of the remaining allocation on line 35 (the Matcher) and noregex puts almost all of it on line 55 (new BigDecimal(p.amount())). Throughput goes up several times and p99.99 drops to tens of microseconds, though the exact numbers vary a lot from run to run on a busy machine. The Kotlin twin's noregex run also shows a site in main's lambda: the call through a (KtPayment) -> Long function type boxes every Long result (22.7% of the remaining allocation in one run).

sections.h: Prove it with JMH, then lock it in with an allocation budget
sections.html:
The investigation found the fix. JMH, from lesson 3, proves it in isolation, with -prof gc. The research run (2 forks of 5 one-second iterations):

Benchmark                 ns/op                   B/op
before                  845.880 ± 338.287    2,032.006 ± 0.002
after1_hoistAndGuard    149.884 ±  50.173      200.001 ± 0.001
after2_noRegex           62.337 ±  16.858       72.000 ± 0.001

FeeBench reproduces it: 2,032.012, 200.002 and 72.001 bytes per call in one run, with time errors larger than some of the scores. The time column tells you the fix helped. The B/op column tells you how much, to the byte. One subtlety: another fork of the same benchmark measured before at 2,112.011 B/op. Each JVM is precise, but two JVMs can differ a little, because the JIT can make different inlining and escape-analysis decisions. Leave room in any threshold.

A benchmark proves the fix today. A test keeps it fixed. The JVM counts the bytes each thread allocates, and com.sun.management.ThreadMXBean.getCurrentThreadAllocatedBytes() reads that counter:

Java
var threads = (com.sun.management.ThreadMXBean) ManagementFactory.getThreadMXBean();
long before = threads.getCurrentThreadAllocatedBytes();
for (int i = 0; i < 100_000; i++) sink += calc.feeCents(ps[i & 1023]);
double perCall = (threads.getCurrentThreadAllocatedBytes() - before) / 100_000.0;
assertThat(perCall).isLessThan(100);         // the budget
Kotlin
val threads = ManagementFactory.getThreadMXBean() as com.sun.management.ThreadMXBean
val before = threads.currentThreadAllocatedBytes
repeat(100_000) { sink += calc.feeCents(ps[it and 1023]) }
val perCall = (threads.currentThreadAllocatedBytes - before) / 100_000.0
assertThat(perCall).isLessThan(100.0)        // the budget

Measure after warm-up, because allocation only settles once C2 has compiled the method and escape analysis has done its work. Measured this way, the slow version settles at 2,131.76 bytes per call. Round 1 settles at 200 bytes on JDK 21, and at 128 on JDK 25. Round 2 is 72 on both. Allocation numbers move with the JDK, so set the budget with a margin, and re-baseline it when you upgrade.

try.title: The proof, in bytes
steps: Predict the B/op of each benchmark in FeeBench, using what the investigation showed.
Run it (about 10 seconds). Compare the error columns for time and for bytes.
Run the Kotlin twin, which measures the Kotlin versions with the per-thread allocation counter, like the lab's test.

code.title: FeeBench.java
code.html: package workbench.performance.l07; import org.openjdk.jmh.annotations.Benchmark; import org.openjdk.jmh.annotations.BenchmarkMode; import org.openjdk.jmh.annotations.Fork; import org.openjdk.jmh.annotations.Measurement; import org.openjdk.jmh.annotations.Mode; import org.openjdk.jmh.annotations.OutputTimeUnit; import org.openjdk.jmh.annotations.Scope; import org.openjdk.jmh.annotations.State; import org.openjdk.jmh.annotations.Warmup; import org.openjdk.jmh.profile.GCProfiler; import org.openjdk.jmh.results.RunResult; import org.openjdk.jmh.runner.Runner; import org.openjdk.jmh.runner.options.OptionsBuilder; import org.openjdk.jmh.runner.options.VerboseMode; import java.util.concurrent.TimeUnit; /** The proof: the three fee versions under JMH with the GC profiler. Bytes per call is the number to keep. */ @State(Scope.Thread) @BenchmarkMode(Mode.AverageTime) @OutputTimeUnit(TimeUnit.NANOSECONDS) @Warmup(iterations = 3, time = 300, timeUnit = TimeUnit.MILLISECONDS) @Measurement(iterations = 3, time = 300, timeUnit = TimeUnit.MILLISECONDS) @Fork(1) public class FeeBench { FeeVariants.Payment payment = new FeeVariants.Payment("pay_123", "EUR", "1234.56", "m_7"); // non-final input @Benchmark public long before() { return FeeVariants.feeSlow(payment); } @Benchmark public long after1Hoisted() { return FeeVariants.feeHoisted(payment); } @Benchmark public long after2NoRegex() { return FeeVariants.feeNoRegex(payment); } public static void main(String[] args) throws Exception { var options = new OptionsBuilder() .include(FeeBench.class.getName()) .addProfiler(GCProfiler.class) .verbosity(VerboseMode.SILENT) .build(); System.out.printf("%-14s %10s %10s %12s %8s%n", "Benchmark", "ns/op", "error", "B/op", "error"); for (RunResult r : new Runner(options).run()) { var time = r.getPrimaryResult(); var bytes = r.getSecondaryResults().get("gc.alloc.rate.norm"); System.out.printf("%-14s %10.1f %10.1f %12.3f %8.3f%n", r.getParams().getBenchmark().replaceAll(".*\\.", ""), time.getScore(), time.getScoreError(), bytes.getScore(), bytes.getScoreError()); } } }

alt.title: FeeBench.kt
alt.html: package workbench.performance.l07 import java.lang.management.ManagementFactory // FeeBench.java proves the fix with JMH, which needs Java classes in this lab. This Kotlin twin // proves it for the Kotlin versions in FeeInvestigation.kt with the per-thread allocation counter, // the same measurement the lab's test uses: warm up, then bytes per call over 100,000 calls. private val counter = ManagementFactory.getThreadMXBean() as com.sun.management.ThreadMXBean private var sink = 0L // results go somewhere the JIT can't ignore private inline fun bytesPerCall(call: () -> Long): Double { // inline: no boxing of the Long var best = Double.MAX_VALUE repeat(10) { // the first rounds include warm-up; keep the best val before = counter.currentThreadAllocatedBytes repeat(100_000) { sink += call() } best = minOf(best, (counter.currentThreadAllocatedBytes - before) / 100_000.0) } return best } fun main() { val p = KtPayment("pay_123", "EUR", "1234.56", "m_7") println("ktFeeSlow: %8.1f B/call".format(bytesPerCall { ktFeeSlow(p) })) println("ktFeeHoisted: %8.1f B/call".format(bytesPerCall { ktFeeHoisted(p) })) println("ktFeeNoRegex: %8.1f B/call".format(bytesPerCall { ktFeeNoRegex(p) })) println("(checksum $sink)") }

try.expect: About 2,000 B/op for before, 200 for after1Hoisted and 72 for after2NoRegex, each with an error well under one byte, while the ns/op errors are large on a busy machine. The Kotlin twin printed 2,080, 280 and 72 bytes per call in one run. The middle number is 80 bytes more than Java's round 1, which is a good reason to measure each language's version instead of assuming they match.

analogy: A performance investigation is like finding why a warehouse's late shipments come in bursts. You don't start by timing the average packer; you look at the late ones and notice they all coincide with the moments the floor is closed for cleaning (the GC pauses). Then you find what makes so much mess: a team that unpacks every box to check one label (the regex), another that prints a report nobody reads (the dropped log line). You fix one team, check the floor again, and only then notice the next mess that was hidden behind the first. The analogy breaks at the end: in a warehouse you'd stop at "less mess". In code you can measure the remaining mess to the byte and fail the build if it grows.
world: Every Quarkus payment service has some version of this code: a validator that compiles a regex per request, BigDecimal constants created inline in fee or FX rules, a log.debug(String.format(...)) or string concatenation in a hot path with DEBUG off in production. When p99 or p99.99 of an endpoint drifts, run the loop: a JFR recording from one pod, gc-pauses and allocation by your own lines, an async-profiler flame graph if you can attach, one fix, a JMH benchmark with -prof gc for the PR, and an allocation budget test so the next refactoring can't silently bring the cost back. Put the JDK version next to the budget: allocation numbers changed between JDK 21 and 25 in this very example.
mistake:
The most common mistake is changing several things at once and declaring victory on the average. Someone hoists the pattern, switches the JSON library and bumps the heap in one PR, the mean latency drops, and nobody knows which change mattered, or whether the tail got better at all. The other mistake is stopping after the first fix: in this investigation the Matcher allocation only became visible after the pattern was hoisted. Fix one thing, measure the tail and the allocation, profile again, and write down each round's numbers.

Java
// "it's precompiled now" is not the end: matcher() still allocates on every call
if (!CCY.matcher(p.currency()).matches()) throw new IllegalArgumentException("bad currency");
Kotlin
// "it's precompiled now" is not the end: matches() still creates a Matcher on every call
require(KT_CCY.matches(p.currency)) { "bad currency" }

compare.title: The fixed fee calculation in Java and Kotlin

java.title: FeeVariants.java
java.html: static final BigDecimal RATE = new BigDecimal("0.029"); // round 1: built once static final BigDecimal FIXED = new BigDecimal("0.30"); static boolean isCurrencyCode(String s) { // round 2: no regex for 3 letters if (s.length() != 3) return false; for (int i = 0; i < 3; i++) { char c = s.charAt(i); if (c < 'A' || c > 'Z') return false; } return true; } static long feeNoRegex(Payment p) { if (!isCurrencyCode(p.currency())) throw new IllegalArgumentException("bad currency"); BigDecimal amount = new BigDecimal(p.amount()); // the work that's left BigDecimal fee = amount.multiply(RATE).add(FIXED).setScale(2, RoundingMode.HALF_EVEN); if (debugEnabled) debug(String.format("payment %s merchant=%s amount=%s fee=%s", // round 1: guarded p.id(), p.merchant(), amount.toPlainString(), fee.toPlainString())); return fee.unscaledValue().longValue(); }

kotlin.title: FeeInvestigation.kt
kotlin.html: val KT_RATE = BigDecimal("0.029") // round 1: built once val KT_FIXED = BigDecimal("0.30") fun isCurrencyCodeKt(s: String) = s.length == 3 && s.all { it in 'A'..'Z' } // round 2: no regex fun ktFeeNoRegex(p: KtPayment): Long { require(isCurrencyCodeKt(p.currency)) { "bad currency" } val amount = BigDecimal(p.amount) // the work that's left val fee = (amount * KT_RATE + KT_FIXED).setScale(2, RoundingMode.HALF_EVEN) if (ktDebugEnabled) ktDebug("payment %s merchant=%s amount=%s fee=%s" // round 1: guarded .format(p.id, p.merchant, amount.toPlainString(), fee.toPlainString())) return fee.unscaledValue().toLong() }

compare.note: After round 2 both versions allocate the same 72 bytes per call, all of it in new BigDecimal(p.amount()). Two Kotlin details showed up on the way. Round 1 measured 280 bytes per call in Kotlin against 200 in Java. Regex.matches delegates to a Matcher just like the Java code, and this course didn't track down the extra 80 bytes, so measure instead of assuming the two versions cost the same. And calling the fee function through a function type, val fee: (KtPayment) -> Long, boxed every Long result: Function1.invoke returns an object. In the noregex run that boxing was 22.7% of the remaining allocation. In hot Kotlin code, call the function directly, pass it to an inline function, or use a fun interface with a primitive return type, the Kotlin counterpart of Java's ToLongFunction.

worked.title: Write up the investigation for the pull request

steps.say: Start with the symptom and how you measured it, with the conditions. Without the conditions, the numbers mean nothing to a reviewer.
steps.code:
Symptom: fee endpoint p99.99 < 13.6 ms (p50 < 0.7 us); 130 GCs / 15 s.
Setup: 4 threads, 15 s, -Xmx256m, JDK 21, 4-vCPU VM, latency histogram per call.

steps.say: Then the evidence for the cause, from two tools, with the lines named.
steps.code:
JFR jdk.ObjectAllocationSample, first frame in our code:
  34.7% Pattern.compile (regex per call)
  31.9% String.format   (DEBUG line, DEBUG off)
  15.9% toPlainString   (arguments of that log line)
   8.9% new BigDecimal("0.029") / ("0.30")
async-profiler alloc: Pattern.compile 37.4%, String.format 27.9% of bytes

steps.say: Then each round separately, with the re-profile that justified the next one. Self-check: why list round 1 even though round 2 includes it? (Because the reviewer should see that the Matcher cost was found by measuring, not guessed, and what each change bought.)
steps.code:
Round 1 (hoist pattern + constants, guard log): p99.99 < 35.6 us, 79 GCs.
  Re-profile: 94.8% of allocation now at CCY.matcher(...).
Round 2 (3-char check instead of regex): p99.99 < 28.4 us, 37 GCs.
  Re-profile: 99.7% at new BigDecimal(p.amount()). Stopping here.

steps.say: End with the proof and the guard: the JMH numbers with errors, and the test that keeps it fixed.
steps.code:
JMH -prof gc (2 forks x 5 x 1 s): before 2,032.006 +/- 0.002 B/op, after 72.000 +/- 0.001 B/op.
FeeCalculatorTest.allocationBudget: < 100 B/call after warm-up (JDK 21 and 25: 72).

lab.title: Bring the fee calculation under its allocation budget
steps: Run the tests. Three pass (fees, currency check, DEBUG message) and one fails: the slow version settles at about 2,130 bytes per call, against a budget of 100.
Optional but worth it: run FeeInvestigation -Pargs=slow and read the allocation by line. Your FeeCalculator has the same three costs.

Round 1: make the pattern and the two BigDecimal constants static final, and format the DEBUG line only when log.isDebugEnabled(). Run the tests. The budget test still fails, now at about 200 bytes (128 on JDK 25). The failure message lists every round it measured.
Round 2: replace the regex with a check that the currency is exactly three characters from A to Z. Run the tests until all four pass.
Keep the fee results, the bad currency message and the exact DEBUG text: the other three tests guard them.
hints: Pattern.compile(...) in a static final field stops the compile, but matcher() still creates a Matcher per call. That's the 128 to 200 bytes left after round 1.
The budget test measures 10 rounds of 100,000 calls and judges the best one, so a slow start while the JIT warms up won't fail it.
For the currency: s.length() == 3 and each charAt(i) between 'A' and 'Z'. Null isn't part of the contract here.
What's left after round 2 is new BigDecimal(p.amount()), about 72 bytes. That's the real work, and it fits the budget.

recap: Start from the tail (p99.9, p99.99) and the GC count. An excellent average can hide calls that wait for GC pauses, and the max is often noise from the machine.
JFR's allocation-by-site names JDK methods; group samples by the first frame in your own code and its line to find what to change. A flame graph confirms who calls it.
Fix one thing at a time and profile again: the order of costs changes, and the Matcher behind a hoisted Pattern only showed up after round 1.
Stop when the top of the profile is the work the code exists to do, here parsing the amount: 72 bytes per call.
Prove it with JMH -prof gc (2,032 to 72 B/op, errors under a byte) and keep it with an allocation budget test that has a margin, because numbers shift between JVMs and JDK versions.

explain.prompt: Explain to a new teammate how you'd investigate "the fee endpoint's p99.99 is bad", from the first measurement to the merged fix, and why each step is there.
explain.answer: First I'd measure the tail properly: percentiles and the GC count under a realistic load, because the average can look perfect while one call in ten thousand waits for a GC pause. If GC is busy, I take a JFR recording and look at gc-pauses and at allocation, grouped by the first frame in our own code, so I get file and line instead of JDK internals. A flame graph confirms who calls the allocating code. Then I fix one thing, the biggest, and measure again, because the order changes and new hot spots appear, like the Matcher behind a hoisted Pattern. I stop when what's left is the real work. Before merging I prove the change with a JMH benchmark using -prof gc, since bytes per operation are stable and time isn't, and I add an allocation budget test with some margin so a later change can't bring the cost back unnoticed.

deeper.html:
The research run also tried one thing worth knowing about latency numbers. Its histogram used fixed buckets (100 ns up to 1 ms, then 100 µs up to 1 s) in a preallocated array, so measuring added no allocation of its own. A latency recorder that allocates per sample would add exactly the garbage you're trying to measure. HdrHistogram is the usual library for this in production.

The flame graph from lesson 6 showed 608 of 8,005 CPU samples in __vdso_clock_gettime: the harness calling System.nanoTime() around every request. Instrumentation has a cost, and on a 60 ns operation it's a large one. That's another reason the final proof is a JMH benchmark rather than the load harness.

For logging in Quarkus, the cheapest disabled log call is one that does nothing before checking the level. JBoss Logging's debugf formats only when DEBUG is on, but the arguments are still evaluated and a varargs call still builds its array. In a hot path, the explicit if (log.isDebugEnabled()) guard is the version you can reason about. A profile will tell you if it matters.

If you want to go below 72 bytes, the remaining cost is BigDecimal parsing. Amounts in cents as long, parsed directly from the request, allocate nothing (lesson 3's MoneyBench measured 0 B/op for the summing part). That trades allocation for code you must keep correct: rounding modes, scale validation, overflow with Math.multiplyExact. Take that trade only if the budget or the profile asks for it.
